title: The Dollar Auction
request: now make a video on this script
sources: Martin Shubik, The Dollar Auction Game: A Paradox in Noncooperative Behavior and Escalation, Journal of Conflict Resolution, March 1971, pages 109 to 111, as quoted word for word by Timothy Taylor, https://conversableeconomist.com/2011/11/15/martin-shubiks-dollar-auction-game/ : the rule (the highest and the second-highest bidder both pay, only the highest gets the dollar); published in 1971; best played during a party when spirits are high; a total of payments between three and five dollars is not uncommon; once two bids are in, the escalation is real. Sure: read through Taylor's quotations; the scan of the paper itself could not be read.

J. Keith Murnighan, A Very Extreme Case of the Dollar Auction, Journal of Management Education, 2002, volume 26, pages 56 to 69, https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2002/a-very-extreme-case-of-the-dollar-auction ; figure as reported by Gillian Ku, https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/research/ktag/resources/papers/ku.pdf : a 20 dollar bill sold for 2,000 dollars in an executive MBA class (a hundred times its worth is 2,000 divided by 20). Fairly sure: three academic summaries agree; the article itself was not opened.

Ned Augenblick, The Sunk-Cost Fallacy in Penny Auctions, Review of Economic Studies, 2016, volume 83, pages 58 to 86, https://kylewoodward.com/blog-data/pdfs/references/augenblick-the-review-of-economic-studies-2015A.pdf : a real penny auction website made about 26 million dollars in profit across 166,000 auctions, September 2005 to June 2009; when it auctioned cash, average revenue was 204% of face value across more than 2,000 cash auctions (about two dollars for every dollar); the paper says the penny auction shares many characteristics with the dollar auction (a close cousin). Sure: the full paper was read.

Barry O'Neill, International Escalation and the Dollar Auction, Journal of Conflict Resolution, 1986, volume 30, pages 33 to 50, https://ideas.repec.org/a/sae/jocore/v30y1986i1p33-50.html : with 2 dollars 50 each, the first bidder should open at 60 cents and the other should stay silent. Sure of the figures, which are in the paper's own abstract; the full article was not opened.

Wikipedia, Dollar auction, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_auction : bids start at a nickel and rise in nickels. Fairly sure: not checked against the original paper; it matches O'Neill's 60 cent answer.
Biku's accuracy notes (script-brief.md): the opening sale (1.85 and 1.80) and every bid the cast makes are an invented scene.
